notes.topic: See how you translate this phrase in Gen 13
notes.text: See how you translate this phrase in Gen 13:10.

Abraham uses **lords** here as a polite address to the three men. The Hebrew word “lord” can also be a reference to God, but notice that at this point Abraham probably thought he was talking to men or angels. It was not until later that he realized that one of them was Yahweh (verse 14). or [Gentlemen]

The pronoun **your** is singular here in the Hebrew text, and also in the next clause. It could be that Abraham is addressing each of the three men simultaneously, or that he is addressing their leader or spokesman. or [if you would honor me with your presence]

People wore sandals, and their feet would get dusty when they traveled. So it was customary to offer guests water to wash the dust off their feet. Also, notice that the pronouns **you** and **your** are plural here in the Hebrew text.
Notice that the pronouns **you** and **your** are plural in this quote in the Hebrew text and refer to Abraham’s three guests.
The word used here in the Hebrew text shows agreement or acceptance. or [That is good]

It is believed that **three seahs** was equivalent to over 20 liters. It was enough flour to make bread for many people, just as the calf (verse 7) provided enough meat for many people and showed generous hospitality. Besides Abraham’s guests, others in his household may have also joined in eating the feast. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this in terms of modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote.

The Hebrew word for **loaves** here is often translated as “cakes,” which probably refers to their flat, round shape (similar to biscuits). However, make sure your translation of this word does not sound like a dessert, because this bread was not sweet. or [and bake some loaves of flat bread] or [and make some bread]

The Hebrew text uses a plural pronoun here (**they**) to refer to one of the three men who spoke to Abraham on behalf of them all (See verse 10). Many languages can use **they** or “the men” in the same way. Make sure your translation of this quote margin does not sound like all three of the men spoke at the same time.
Make sure it is clear in your translation that Abraham is the one speaking here.
For some languages it may be more natural to move this time phrase to the beginning of this quote and say, “Next year at this time I will surely return …” or [next year at this time]
This sentence gives information about something that was happening while the man was talking. Translate this in a way that makes that clear in your language. or [Sarah was eavesdropping]

The Hebrew text has an idiom here that is a polite way of saying that Sarah had reached menopause and so was not able to have children. Other languages may have a similar idiom. Make sure your translation of this clause will not offend or embarrass people when it is read aloud in public. or [so that she was far past the time that she could bear children]

notes.topic: or [Now that I am too old to conceive]
notes.text: or [Now that I am too old to conceive]

Yahweh uses rhetorical question in verses 13–14 to confront Sarah’s disbelief and to emphasize that nothing is too difficult for God to do. Consider whether or not it is best to use rhetorical questions here in your language. or [Sarah should not have laughed and thought to herself] or [Sarah should not have laughed, thinking]

Also, for some languages it may be better to put this phrase right after the first time phrase in this verse and say, “At the time that I have decided, which will be this time next year, I will return here to visit you,” or [—it will be at this time next year—]
The Hebrew verb here includes the meaning of lying or deceiving.

The expression **will be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God.
Consider whether or not your language has an idiom that fits well here.
Make sure it is clear in your translation that Yahweh is speaking about himself here.
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh here. Make sure the way you use nouns and pronouns throughout this verse makes it clear in your language who is speaking and who is being referred to.

notes.text: Make sure it is clear in your translation that the phrase **Sodom and Gomorrah** refers to the people in those cities. Also, in the Hebrew text this sentence continues into verse 21. or [I have heard many people crying out against the people in the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah because they are committing very evil things]

Abraham uses a rhetorical question here to express his strong feelings and concern about what Yahweh told him. Consider whether or not it is clear and natural to use a rhetorical question here in your language. Make sure it does not sound like Abraham is angry or being rude. or [Surely you would not destroy]

This idiom expresses emphatically that Abraham does not believe Yahweh would do this. Consider whether or not your language has a similar idiom. Make sure that Abraham sounds respectful in your translation. or [It seems impossible that you would ever] or [I hope that you would never]

The idiom **taken it upon myself** means that Abraham has decided to do something and is acting boldly. Consider whether or not your language has an idiom that fits well here. or [Please excuse me for speaking to you so boldly]

Even though Abraham realizes by now that he is talking to Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **my lord** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Use a respectful term in your translation that is appropriate for him to use when he refers to Yahweh here and in the rest of this chapter. or [Master]
or [I am nothing compared to you] or [I have no status compared to you]
Make sure it is clear in your translation that Yahweh is speaking here, not Abraham. or [Yahweh answered him]
Make sure it is clear in your translation that Abraham is speaking here, not Yahweh. or [Then Abraham pleaded with Yahweh]

Even though Abraham is addressing Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **my Lord** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person.
Make sure it is clear in your translation that Yahweh is speaking here, not Abraham. or [He answered him]
Make sure it is clear in your translation that Abraham is speaking here, not Yahweh. or [Then Abraham asked Yahweh]
or [My Lord please excuse me for speaking to you so boldly]
Consider again how you translated **my Lord** in verses 27, 30–32. Contrast that to verse 3, where Abraham probably used the term before he realized that he was talking to Yahweh.
